passage: In the school van home through Chennai traffic, Devika had everyone laughing. 'Why did the St. Mark's student stare at the orange juice box? Because it said concentrate.' Then the one about them being a herd of donkeys who needed a map to find the canteen. The jokes had been going round her class all week, ever since the inter-school quiz. At home she repeated them at the dinner table, loudly, while Manjula Aunty from next door was there borrowing sugar. Manjula Aunty laughed politely once, then stopped. 'I teach Class 9 at St. Mark's,' she said. 'There's a girl there, Kavitha, who stays after school every day to help her brother with maths. Which one is the donkey?' Devika went red. 'It's not about real people, Aunty. It's just... them.' 'Them is always real people,' Manjula Aunty said, and picked up her sugar.

qa.q: Which class does Manjula Aunty teach at St. Mark's?
qa.a: Manjula Aunty teaches Class 9 at St. Mark's.

qa.q: Why does Devika say 'It's not about real people'?
qa.a: Thinking of St. Mark's students as a faceless 'them' lets Devika laugh without picturing anyone being hurt, so the jokes feel harmless.

qa.q: What did Manjula Aunty do that made the jokes harder to laugh at?
qa.a: She named one real student, Kavitha, and a detail of her life, which gave the group a face and showed the 'donkeys' were real people.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel if she heard these jokes?
qa.a: Kavitha, who stays late to help her brother, would likely feel hurt and insulted to be lumped into a herd of 'donkeys' by people who have never met her.

grounding: Shows a teenager repeating jokes that call a rival school's students stupid donkeys, until a neighbour who teaches there names one of them.

'Tarun, what's this?' Anand held up Tarun's phone, the class group open.
'Give it back, bhaiya. It's just memes.'
'A picture of rats with "Nala Colony school trip" written on it. Just memes?'
'Everyone sends them. They are like rats, though. They live in that dump across the nala.'
'Shabnam from Nala Colony tutors you in chemistry on Sundays.'
'...That's different.'
'How?'
'She's, like, a person. I know her.'
'And the others aren't people because you don't know them?'
Tarun grabbed the phone, then didn't open it. 'You're making it a big deal.'
'I'm asking you to picture Shabnam scrolling this group.'
Tarun sat down. After a long minute he typed, 'guys this is too much, delete it,' and put the phone face down.

qa.q: Who tutors Tarun in chemistry on Sundays?
qa.a: Shabnam from Nala Colony tutors Tarun on Sundays.

qa.q: Why does Tarun say Shabnam is 'different'?
qa.a: Tarun feels uncomfortable because he knows Shabnam as a person who can't fit the 'rats' joke; the others stay faceless, which is what makes the cruelty feel easy.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the talk?
qa.a: Anand asking Tarun to picture Shabnam scrolling the group made the target real, and Tarun chose to tell the group to delete the meme.

qa.q: How might Shabnam feel if she saw the meme?
qa.a: Shabnam would likely feel hurt and humiliated to see her home called a rat colony by students she might even teach.

grounding: Shows a teenager sharing memes that call a poorer colony's residents rats, until his brother makes him picture one real person from there.

subtype: Mocking a group as not real people [Actor]
passage: In Class 11 our school cricket team had a running joke about the boys from the Hill Road academy. We called them 'the cattle'. I, Dhruv, made up half the jokes: they moo instead of appealing, they need a farmer to set the field. It was easy to laugh, because they weren't really people to us, just a colour of jersey. Then at the district camp I was paired with Manoj from Hill Road for fielding drills. He was funny. He carried spare grips for everyone. On the last day he said, 'You're the one who does the cattle jokes, right? My little brother cried about that video.' I didn't know what to say. That's when I understood how the jokes had worked: as long as they had no faces, I didn't have to feel anything. I stopped making them. I still think about his brother.

qa.q: What did Manoj carry for everyone at the camp?
qa.a: Manoj carried spare grips for everyone.

qa.q: Why was it easy for Dhruv to laugh at the 'cattle' jokes?
qa.a: The Hill Road boys were just a jersey colour to Dhruv, so Dhruv felt no guilt or sympathy, as the cruelty didn't seem to land on anyone.

qa.q: What changed Dhruv's behaviour?
qa.a: Getting to know Manoj, and hearing that his little brother cried over a video, gave the group real faces, and Dhruv stopped making the jokes.

qa.q: What might Manoj have been feeling when he mentioned his brother?
qa.a: Manoj may have felt hurt on his brother's behalf and a bit wary, but chose to say it calmly after days of friendly drills.

grounding: Shows someone looking back on making jokes that called a rival academy's players cattle, until meeting one of them made the group real.

subtype: Mocking a group as not real people [Actor]
passage:
Youth group note, parish hall, Margao. Reena (leader).
Friday. During the snack break, Joseph (15) had the group laughing about the workers building the new flats next door: 'They're donkeys, na? Twenty of them in one room, can't even read a sign.' He made braying noises when one of them walked past the gate. Two younger boys copied him.
I noticed he never used a single name. When I asked whether he knew any of them, he shrugged: 'They're all the same.'
What I did: on Sunday I asked the site supervisor if one of the workers would share lunch with us. Dinesh came, from a village two days away by train, and passed round a photo of his daughter's school certificate. Joseph asked him three questions and didn't bray once.
Plan: Joseph has offered to help with the Sunday reading class for the workers' children. I'll check in with him about how it goes.

qa.q: What sound did Joseph make when a worker walked past the gate?
qa.a: He made braying noises.

qa.q: Why did the jokes feel harmless to Joseph at the time?
qa.a: Joseph felt amused, seeing the workers as 'all the same', a faceless crowd rather than people, so mocking them felt like a laugh rather than cruelty.

qa.q: Which step of Reena's changed Joseph's behaviour, and why?
qa.a: Inviting Dinesh to share lunch; once Joseph met one real person with a name and a daughter's certificate, the braying stopped and questions took its place.

qa.q: What would change for the two younger boys if Reena had not stepped in?
qa.a: They would likely learn that mocking the workers wins laughs, and keep seeing the people next door as animals rather than neighbours.

grounding: A youth leader notes a teenager who calls a group of workers donkeys and never names them, and how meeting one of them changes things.

subtype: Mocking a group as not real people [Actor]
passage:
Thursday, 9:40 p.m.
Inter-school quiz today. The government school team sat across from us in the hall, and at the break Mitali said, 'Look, the buffalo herd has arrived.' I added, 'Mooing the answers, probably,' and our whole bench cracked up. I kept the mooing going all lunch. It was honestly funny.
Then they beat us in the final round. Their captain, Sunaina, got the one about monsoon winds before I'd even touched the buzzer.
At the handshake she said, 'Good match, Nandini,' because she'd read my name tag. I didn't know hers until the announcer said it.
I can't stop thinking about that. She looked at me like a person, and all day I'd been making cow noises at her.
Not writing any more tonight.

qa.q: Who answered the question about monsoon winds?
qa.a: Sunaina, the captain of the government school team.

qa.q: What is Nandini feeling at the end of the entry, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nandini feels uneasy and ashamed: the entry says Nandini 'can't stop thinking' about Sunaina using a name after a day of cow noises, and it ends abruptly.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nandini's day, and what could Nandini do now?
qa.a: The handshake, when Sunaina used Nandini's name; Nandini could drop the mooing jokes and learn the names of the other team's players.

qa.q: How might the lunch-break jokes have looked from the government school bench?
qa.a: They may have heard a whole bench mooing at them and felt dismissed as a herd, not seen as a quiz team, which they then proved in the final round.

grounding: A teenager who joins jokes calling another school's team a buffalo herd is shaken when one of them greets the teenager by name.
